subject: 🗣️ Warsh's comms task
body_html:
Plus: Big central bank week | Monday, September 14, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Sep 14, 2026

It's a big week for global central banking, with meetings of the Federal Reserve, Bank of England and Bank of Japan all on tap.

  • Below, we look at the overseas monetary policy action. But first, a look at what markets will be listening for from Fed chairman Kevin Warsh as he seeks to avoid a repeat of July's press conference performance.

Situational awareness: The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield surpassed 5% this morning for the first time since 2023, extending a melt-up in long-term borrowing costs. If the yield ends the day above that level, it will be the first time since 2007. 😬

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Amy Stern, is 974 words, a 3½-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: How Warsh can avoid a repeat of July's communications mess
 

Fed chairman Kevin Warsh at a July news conference. Photo: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Seven weeks ago, Warsh took questions from the media, and it didn't go well. Markets sold off as he seemed vague and evasive about the reasoning behind the latest interest rate decision. Wednesday, he gets a do-over.

Why it matters: Investors will be thirsty for a more detailed explanation of the Fed's decision than the one Warsh offered in late July — even while respecting his intention not to give explicit guidance about future policy moves.

  • Markets are pricing in a quarter-point increase in rates — but the why behind that likely move is more significant than the act itself, for what it says about the Fed's analytical framework under its new leadership.
  • And if the Fed's policymaking Federal Open Market Committee elects to leave rates unchanged, Warsh will have an even trickier communications task, lest the bond market again start to question Warsh's willingness to use interest rate policy to keep inflation in check.

State of play: Assuming the Fed raises rates, does it reflect a belief that seemingly one-off changes to prices from tariffs and the energy shock are turning out to be more prolonged than previously thought?

  • Or is AI-fueled investment creating more sustained inflationary pressure? Is it simply that the neutral interest rate is higher than it seemed?
  • Not all interest rate adjustments are created equal. A "mid-cycle adjustment," like the three rate cuts enacted in 2019, or a "recalibration" or an "insurance move" imply different things from something like a "normalization" or a sustained policy tightening.

Between the lines: Of course, each of these potential answers has implications for what the Fed will do next, in tension with Warsh's deeply held desire to avoid anything resembling "forward guidance."

  • Moreover, different officials on the policy committee may have different rationales for a rate hike (or for not hiking), and as chairman Warsh has an obligation to accurately describe the range of views.
  • But there's a pick-your-poison dilemma he faces. If the Fed chairman fails to lay out a coherent framework and rationale for a policy move (or no move), people naturally start to wonder if there is one.

What they're saying: "We expect that he will frame the hike as a way to ensure that inflation returns to target in an acceptable timeframe," Christopher Hodge and Selin Aker at Natixis wrote in a note out this morning.

  • "We also think that he will emphasize that this decision was discrete and does not pre-commit the Fed to any actions in subsequent meetings, giving him and the Committee maximum flexibility to respond to shocks."

The bottom line: They teach us in the journalism business to ask the "who, what, when, where and why." At Wednesday's press conference, the first four will already be known.

  • Who = Kevin Warsh and the FOMC; what = an interest rate move or no move announced half an hour earlier; when = 2:30pm ET; where = the William McChesney Martin Jr. Building.
  • That leaves "why," which is the question that traders worldwide will be most eager to hear.

2. 🌏 Global tightening on tap
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

It's not just the Fed. Global monetary policy is abruptly swinging back to tightening mode, with some central banks facing tests to their credibility.

Driving the news: The European Central Bank raised rates last week, and the Fed may follow suit, as we note above.

  • 🇯🇵 The Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise interest rates on Friday, accelerating a tightening campaign that began in 2024.
  • 🇬🇧 The Bank of England is expected to hold rates steady Thursday, but the focus will be on what governor Andrew Bailey signals about further hikes as inflation pressures build.

The intrigue: The BOJ is being pulled in opposite directions as persistent inflation strengthens the case for higher rates.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has pressed Japan to raise rates after the U.S. intervened to prop up the yen this summer.
  • He has warned traders against betting on renewed weakness, hinting that Washington knew tighter policy was coming: "I am the house now."

On the other side is Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who favors easy monetary policy (though her administration appears accepting of the need for further hikes).

  • Higher rates could help contain inflation and support the yen, though that would also raise borrowing costs and make it harder for Takaichi to deliver on her economic agenda.

What to watch: Higher rates — signals that central banks are prepared to do more — could paradoxically help chill the surge in global borrowing costs if financial markets are convinced inflation will be contained.

Of note: The European Central Bank's renewed inflation fight may soon come alongside a change at the top.

  • A six-byline scoop by the Financial Times shows that a multinational horse-trading is underway over who will replace ECB president Christine Lagarde when she departs, as is widely expected, in the months ahead. National rivalries are complicating who will get the job.
  • European officials hope to strike a "grand package" by year-end, balancing national claims across the ECB presidency, chief economist and another executive board seat, the FT reports.
  • For example, Berlin sees a non-German president paired with a powerful German chief economist as one possible deal.
